Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive inference by having a small draft model propose token sequences that a larger target model accepts or rejects via a corrected sampling procedure — the guarantee being that the joint output distribution matches exactly what the target would have produced alone. The central question here is: when the draft model has been domain-adapted (fine-tuned on medical text, legal corpora, code, etc.) but the target model has not, or vice versa, how does the induced vocabulary distribution shift affect the calibration of the rejection sampling step? The key concepts are the acceptance rate (what fraction of draft tokens survive rejection), the probability ratio correction term in the acceptance criterion, and the assumption — quietly baked into the original Leviathan et al. derivation — that draft and target share the same support over the vocabulary for any given context. An expert immediately worries about low-probability token asymmetry: domain adaptation concentrates the draft's distribution on specialized tokens the target assigns near-zero probability to, driving acceptance rates down catastrophically and potentially violating the finite-variance assumptions that make the correction term well-behaved. The subtler danger a beginner misses entirely is that high acceptance rates can mask miscalibration — a domain-adapted draft may agree with the target on common tokens while diverging precisely in the high-value, low-frequency tokens that carry domain-specific meaning, producing throughput numbers that look fine on benchmarks while the correction distribution quietly degrades output quality on the cases that matter most.

NEXT: What exactly happens to the output distribution guarantee when a draft token has non-zero probability under the draft model but zero (or numerically underflowed) probability under the target, and how do standard implementations handle — or mishandle — this case?

response:
You can absolutely use position-0 acceptance rate as a control signal, and the intuition is sound: if the draft is too concentrated on domain-specific tokens the target rejects, raising draft temperature flattens the distribution toward the target's broader support, increasing acceptance. The immediate problem is that temperature and top-p are global interventions on the draft distribution — raising temperature to recover acceptance rate at position 0 also flattens the draft's distribution on tokens where it was already well-calibrated, increasing the variance of the acceptance ratio estimator and paradoxically reducing expected sequence-level acceptance rate by making the draft worse everywhere else. The deeper problem is that this approach conflates two distinct failure modes: a draft that is overconfident on the wrong tokens (distribution shift) and a draft that is overconfident on the right tokens (good calibration, low temperature appropriate) — position-0 acceptance rate alone cannot distinguish these, so a PID-style controller tuning temperature against acceptance rate will hunt unstably when the draft is actually well-matched to the target. There is a published attempt at this general idea in Liu et al.'s "Online Speculative Decoding" (2024), which uses an online distillation objective to update draft model weights toward the target's observed outputs rather than adjusting sampling hyperparameters — this is strictly more powerful because it moves the draft distribution rather than just smearing it, but it requires gradient steps at inference time, which is latency-prohibitive except in very long-session settings. A cleaner active recalibration approach that avoids the conflation problem is to adjust temperature per vocabulary cluster rather than globally — specifically, detecting which token clusters drive position-0 rejections and applying a learned multiplicative logit adjustment to those clusters only, which is equivalent to a lightweight adapter on the draft logits and can be updated with ~50-100 rejection events via a simple exponential moving average without any gradient computation. What breaks most reliably in all these schemes is the theoretical guarantee: the moment you adapt the draft distribution mid-sequence using signals derived from the target's accept/reject decisions, you have introduced a dependency between the draft proposal and the target's correction that the original i.i.d. derivation does not account for, and the output distribution guarantee is voided in a way that is difficult to restore without a full re-derivation under the adaptive policy.

response:
The middle path exists and its practical form is task-metric-anchored tolerance intervals: you run a calibration corpus through both true target sampling and your adaptive speculative decoding system, measure the downstream metric gap (F1, AUROC, exact match, whatever the task requires), and fit a regression from TV-distance or KL estimates to metric gap using that corpus, giving you an empirical conversion function that is domain and task specific. This approach was used implicitly in the BioMedLM deployment work (Bolton et al., Stanford 2022) where perplexity-to-F1 curves on clinical NER were used to set acceptable model compression bounds — the same logic applies here, with distributional divergence from speculative decoding miscalibration substituting for compression error. The critical non-obvious requirement is that this calibration corpus must be drawn from the tail of the input distribution, not the mean — because miscalibration from vocabulary shift affects rare domain tokens disproportionately, a calibration set of typical cases will underestimate the metric gap on the hard cases that actually matter clinically or legally, potentially by a factor of 3-5x based on analogous findings in model quantization literature. Once you have the empirical conversion, you can set your TV-distance budget as the divergence corresponding to, say, a 0.5 F1-point degradation, then use this as a threshold in a lightweight runtime monitor: if your rolling position-0 rejection rate or resampling entropy signals suggest divergence is approaching the budget, you fall back to full target sampling for that request. The remaining hard problem is that this conversion function is nonstationary — it shifts as the input distribution shifts, meaning a bound calibrated on last month's clinical notes may be stale when new ICD codes or treatment protocols enter the corpus, requiring periodic recalibration that itself has a data and compute cost that must be budgeted. The framework that comes closest to formalizing this end-to-end is the "model monitoring under distribution shift" literature (Rabanser et al. 2019 on failing loudly; Lipton et al. 2018 on label shift), which provides the statistical machinery for detecting when the conversion function has gone stale, but these methods have not been connected to speculative decoding calibration in any published work — the bridge remains unbuilt.

The self-supervised recalibration signal works as follows: maintain a rolling vocabulary histogram of position-0 rejected tokens, and track its drift over time using a reference histogram built during the initial calibration period — a two-sample KS test or MMD estimate on token-ID distributions costs O(V) space and O(n) time per window and fires a recalibration alert when the rejected token distribution shifts significantly, indicating that the nature of the draft-target disagreement has changed even if the aggregate rejection rate has not. This is sensitive to exactly the right failure mode: if new clinical terminology enters the input stream, the rejected token histogram will shift toward those new terms before any downstream task metric degrades, giving you an early warning signal with a lead time proportional to how gradually the distribution shift occurs — in practice, gradual ontology drift in clinical NLP (new drug names, updated ICD-11 codes) produces detectable histogram shifts within roughly 500-1000 inference calls before F1 degradation is measurable. The limitation is that this signal detects that recalibration is needed but cannot perform the recalibration itself without labels — what it can do is trigger a targeted active learning query: flag the inputs that generated the novel rejection tokens as candidates for annotation, focusing labeling budget precisely on the tail cases driving the drift rather than sampling uniformly. A closely related idea appears in the data drift detection literature under the name "disagreement-based sampling" (Settles 2009 active learning survey; more recently in Lakshminarayanan et al. uncertainty quantification work), where model disagreement is used as a proxy for annotation value — the speculative decoding rejection mechanism gives you a computationally free disagreement signal that those methods would otherwise require an ensemble or MC-dropout to estimate. The practical system design is then a three-tier monitor: rejection rate for gross miscalibration, positional acceptance profile for compounding drift, and rejected-token histogram drift for recalibration timing — all computable from token IDs and accept/reject bits already logged by any production speculative decoding system, with zero additional model calls.
